The street was wrong by three feet, and that was how it began. It was a small lane in Chitpur, no wider than a handcart and its driver, and on the map Amrita Sen had drawn the previous week it had run straight from the mouth of Kumudini Gali to the drain behind the clockmaker’s shop. Today, when she laid her new tracing over the old sheet, the lane had bowed to the east, as if some unseen hand had pushed its middle aside while leaving its ends fastened. Three feet. Not enough for a wall to lean. Not enough for a surveyor to mistake. Enough, if she was careful, to make a city different.

The map room of the Bengal Survey Office was a long room under a verandah of dark wood. Its windows opened onto the Maidan, where the grass lay flattened by the heat and the dust of the road moved in thin gold waves. On the floor, a ceiling fan ticked and coughed in its brass socket. Along the table, the maps of Kolkata—Calcutta, as the ledger books still insisted—spread in blue and ink: the Howrah crossing not yet a bridge but a promise of piers, the tram lines a child’s game of connect-the-dots, the old town a web of names that changed with every landlord, every sale, every new drain. Amrita worked at the far end, where the light was less direct and the paper did not yellow so quickly. As assistant cartographer, she was the only woman in the office, and after two years the other men had stopped announcing it. They still announced it by not hearing it.

Her ink was still wet on the Chitpur plan when Bishnu Ghosh came in with a cup of tea and the morning’s theodolite sheets. He was young, with a neat moustache and a fear of ink that made him hold his paper one inch from every blotter.
‘Begum,’ he said, ‘Mr. Haldane asks if the Chitpur plan will be ready by noon.’
‘No,’ Amrita said.
‘No? But you have it nearly finished.’
‘I have it finished in the way that a broken clock is finished. It is always correct twice a day.’
Bishnu did not laugh. He set the tea on the edge of the table, careful of the maps.
‘What is the trouble? The lane by the clockmaker’s?’
‘The lane by the clockmaker’s.’
She lifted the old tracing with two fingers and laid it over the new sheet. The paper was thin as onion skin. Beneath it, the streets of Chitpur lined up in pairs, the same angles, the same stubborn right turns. Only Kumudini Gali would not sit. It had moved east by three feet. The archive told the same story: every revision since 1884 had shown the lane in a different place, each time chalked up to surveyor’s error. The drain was in the same place. The mouth of the lane was in the same place. The houses either side stood in their original positions, as she had measured them from the corner stones. Yet the street between them had shifted, like a needle bent in a frame while the frame remained true.
‘Perhaps your compass was off,’ Bishnu said.
‘My compass was on the table. I checked it three times. I checked it against the baseline from the stone pillar at the corner. I checked it against the drain, which is older than the pillar and has no business moving.’
‘And the houses?’
‘The houses are where I put them.’
‘But the street is not.’
‘No.’
‘Is it possible the drain has moved?’
‘If the drain has moved, then I am a very careless woman and the city is very careless with its own sewers.’
Bishnu looked at the overlay.
‘It is only three feet.’
‘Exactly three feet,’ Amrita said. ‘Which is why I cannot ignore it.’

Mr. Haldane came in at ten with his hat still on, because he had come from the carriage. He was a compact Scotsman with a ledger mind and a habit of saying ‘now’ at the end of sentences as if time were a clerk to be dismissed.
‘Now, Miss Sen, you have been holding the Chitpur plan for three days. The Municipal Commissioner requires the new drains. If a lane is uncertain, mark it uncertain. If a drain is uncertain, mark it uncertain. If a man is uncertain, mark him uncertain. The map is not a place where uncertainty can live forever.’
‘Mr. Haldane, Kumudini Gali has moved.’
‘Calcutta moves every day. Houses fall. Streets are opened. A lane may be widened for the police line.’
‘The houses have not moved.’
‘Then the houses are wrong.’
‘No, the houses are right. I measured them this morning from the same stones I measured them last week. The street has moved between them.’
He looked at Bishnu, then at the overlay.
‘You have made a mistake in the old tracing.’
‘The old tracing is from the office archive. It was drawn by Mr. Rea in 1884. He is dead. If he made a mistake, he made it for nine years.’
‘Rea was a good surveyor.’
‘Rea was a dead surveyor. Which makes his work easier to correct.’
Haldane’s jaw moved.
‘You are proposing that a street in Chitpur moves overnight.’
‘I am proposing that on my map it does. I intend to find out why.’
‘And what do you intend to do?’
‘Walk it. Again. And if it has not moved, I will draw it straight and apologize to the Commissioner. If it has moved, I will draw it where it is. A map that tells lies to keep the peace is not a map. It is a flag.’

By eleven she was outside. The office had given her a note for the watchman at the gate and a compass case that had belonged to a retired inspector. She took a measuring tape, a notebook, and a stick with a brass tip. Bishnu wanted to come; she told him if the street was moving, it was not because of an assistant. He looked hurt but sensible.
The lane began at the corner where the brick press sold its grey blocks in neat columns. A boy in a white cap sold jalebis in a blackened pan. The smell of sugar and ghee rose in a bright column. The pavement was uneven, with a lip of brick worn smooth by bare feet and goat hooves. Amrita walked slowly, laying her tape from the corner stone to the first house. Eight feet. To the second. Nine. To the drain. Forty-three. She wrote the numbers in a small book with a leather cover, the same book in which she kept her salary, her complaints, and a list of men who had called her ‘very clever for a girl’ and the exact dates they had said it.
At the drain, she stopped. The water was black and slow, with a leaf floating in a ring of oil. The mouth of the lane was behind her, forty-three feet away, exactly as it had been in the morning. She turned and looked down the street. It was the same street. It was not the same street. The bend was there, faint, as if the lane had been straight the previous week and now admitted a shoulder. She stood in the middle and listened. A cart passed outside. A bell rang from a school. Somewhere in a house a woman called a name, and the name was answered, and the ordinary world continued, indifferent to a three-foot rebellion.
She sat on an upturned crate near the clockmaker’s shop and opened her notebook. The shop’s windows were full of brass clocks with broken faces. One ticked. Another ticked against it, out of time. An old man watched her from inside.
‘You are drawing our street?’ he said in Bengali.
‘I am measuring it.’
‘Why?’
‘Because it has moved.’
The old man laughed.
‘The street does not move. The city moves. The street stays where you need it.’
